findings.summary: isPublished(article) does `if (article.draft)` with no guard for `article` being undefined. articles.get(slug) returns undefined for any /blog/<slug> link whose slug isn't a file in packages/content/articles (a typo, a renamed/deleted post, a link added before its target file exists). Reproduced directly: running the plugin on a link to `/blog/this-slug-does-not-exist` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'draft')`, which crashes the entire Astro build rather than being logged/handled. No current content triggers this (I diffed all /blog/ links in packages/content/articles against actual slugs — all resolve today), but it's a live landmine for the very next slug rename or typo.

findings.summary: The implementer's report states 'Tests for the change were written and run,' but the diff contains no test file, and the repo has no test runner configured at all (no test script in apps/web/package.json, no *.test.* files anywhere in the repo). The claim is unverifiable at best and false at worst — and my own manual exercise of the shipped code immediately found the crash bug above, which any real test would have caught.

findings.summary: The brief asks for 'the same not-draft-and-not-future-dated rule the rest of the site applies,' but the canonical apps/web/src/utils/data-utils.ts isPublished() is `!data.draft && (import.meta.env.DEV || dateCheck)` — it bypasses the future-date check entirely in dev mode so authors can preview scheduled posts locally. This plugin's isPublished() has no DEV bypass, so during `astro dev` a future-dated post shows normally in the index/tags/rss (via the real isPublished) while any internal link to it still gets stripped to plain text — a live inconsistency during local preview, not just an edge case.

findings.summary: loadArticles() does a synchronous readdirSync plus readFileSync/parse of every article file on every single processed document (every article/project/page in the build), rather than being read once per build. Cheap at today's ~17 articles, but it's unnecessary repeated I/O that a module-level cache would avoid for free.
